“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

“If ⁠they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank’,” he said.

Trump made the post as a trade dispute between Washington and Ottawa esclates, part of the near-global tariff wall in his second term ⁠that has drawn complaints from many US trading partners. Canada is set to introduce a wave of counter-tariffs against the US on Tuesday.

Bombardier, the Montreal-based rival of US business jet manufacturer Gulfstream Aerospace, has an American workforce of 3,500, and a US footprint of 2,800 suppliers, along with factories and service centers in the country.

The company is now adding its sixth US service center and produces wings for its flagship Global 8000 jet in Texas.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

New Hampshire and Rhode Island primary voters will choose candidates across a full slate of federal, state and local offices over the next two days.

In New Hampshire, US senator Jeanne Shaheen’s decision to not seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races, AP reported. Two of the eight Republicans hoping to replace the three-term Democrat are former US senators she previously defeated: John E. Sununu and Scott Brown.

The five-way race for the Democratic nomination includes US representative Chris Pappas, whose departure from his 1st congressional district seat in turn attracted a crowd of candidates.

Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, is among those seeking the Democratic nomination for Pappas’ seat, along with former candidate Maura Sullivan. Several other candidates in top races also are making repeat appearances.

Meanwhile, in Rhode Island, governor Dan McKee faces a tough Democratic primary challenge tomorrow in his bid for a second full term. Voters will also choose nominees for a full slate of federal, state and local offices.

McKee was elected governor by a wide margin in 2022 after first assuming the role in March 2021 when then-governor Gina Raimondo stepped down to become US commerce secretary. He now is at risk of becoming the nation’s first elected governor since 2014 to lose renomination and the first in Rhode Island since 1994.

His challenger is Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a former longtime executive with Rhode Island-based CVS. She placed a close second behind McKee in the five-way 2022 Democratic primary. She is the niece of former Democratic senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut.

President Donald Trump said on Monday that ⁠Canadian private jet maker Bombardier would ⁠no longer be allowed ​to sell its planes in the United States unless it started manufacturing in the country. “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “If ⁠they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ’piggybank’.”

New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to come face-to-face with Rudy Giuliani at the main September 11 memorial service, just days after the former mayor – who led the city at the time of the 2001 terrorist attacks – disparaged his Muslim religion and said he should skip the ceremony. In an interview with right-leaning Newsmax at the weekend, Giuliani said: “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US. Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently released a report linking “gender ideology” to leftwing authoritarianism and political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted and “nakedly political”, likely leading to greater politicization of science and health. It follows attempts by the administration to limit access to gender-affirming care – including, on Friday, an agreement reached between the Department of Justice and a New York hospital to no longer offer pediatric gender-affirming care.

articles.title: Fourteen men go on trial in Paris over deadliest small-boat Channel crossing
articles.excerpt:
Sinking of inflatable dinghy in 2021 resulted in 31 people dead or missing, including a seven-year-old child

Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris over the deaths of at least 31 people in the wors...
articles.body_text:
Sinking of inflatable dinghy in 2021 resulted in 31 people dead or missing, including a seven-year-old child

Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris over the deaths of at least 31 people in the worst mass drowning from a small-boat crossing in the Channel on record.

The accused men, alleged to be linked to people-smuggling networks, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.

Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.

The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead also included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.

A team on a French fishing boat near British waters off Calais had raised the alarm when they saw several lifeless bodies floating in the water.

According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes – between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England – began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.

Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived the tragedy.

Investigators allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.

Two of them, including an Afghan man, are the subject of arrest warrants and will be tried in absentia.

Among the defendants are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators connected to the ​smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched.

Prosecutors have accused the defendants of helping launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.

Liability has also been extended to those accused of transporting, housing or accompanying the victims, actions that formed part of a “chain of successive events” leading to the tragedy, according to investigators.

The defendants have denied being smugglers and disputed their responsibility, or have presented themselves as people who were seeking to make the journey themselves.

However, phone records and location tracking placed several of them near the departure site and linked them to organising crossings to Britain.

For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by the French fishing vessel.

A separate investigation is ongoing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel – who have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.

The UK’s Cranston inquiry, in its report released in February, found that systemic failings, missed opportunities and inadequate resourcing undermined the UK’s maritime search and rescue response on the night of the disaster. HM Coastguard was placed in an “intolerable position”, it said, with chronic staff shortages and limited operational capacity contributing directly to the failure to rescue people in the water.

It found the deaths would have been “avoidable” if British and French authorities had acted sooner to rescue those onboard.

Families ​of some of the victims will travel from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to attend part of the trial, their lawyers said.

“Justice must hold accountable everyone who played a role in this tragedy,” the lawyers, Matthieu Chirez, Thomas Ricard and Camille Renouard, said in a statement.

Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Congress spends $7 trillion. Here’s how that math works out if you think of just $100
articles.excerpt: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss the GOP's legislative priorities, the SAVE America Act and the national debt surpassing $40 trillion ahead of the upcoming midte...
articles.body_text:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss the GOP's legislative priorities, the SAVE America Act and the national debt surpassing $40 trillion ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

You work. You get paid. Washington takes its cut. But have you ever stopped to ask one simple question: Where does the money actually go?

Forget trillion-dollar numbers for a minute. Most Americans can't comprehend the difference between $1 trillion and $7 trillion anyway. Let's shrink Washington down to something we all understand: a $100 bill.

In fiscal year 2025, the federal government spent roughly $7 trillion. Social Security alone consumed about $1.6 trillion. Major federal health programs, including Medicare and Medicaid, were another enormous piece. Defense approached $900 billion.

WASHINGTON IS DRIVING AMERICA TOWARD A DEBT CRISIS WE CAN'T IGNORE ANY LONGER

And then there's the number that should make every taxpayer spit out their morning coffee: interest.

Congressional overspending is only part of the budget problem. (Douglas Rissing)

The federal government spent about $970 billion just on net interest on the national debt. Not roads. Not teachers. Not soldiers. Not Social Security checks.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM?

That means roughly $14 out of every $100 Washington spent went toward interest on money we've already borrowed.

‘THE ODYSSEY’ REMINDS US OF THE NIGHTMARE WE ARE LEAVING FOR AMERICAN CHILDREN

Think about your own household budget. Imagine earning $100 and immediately throwing $14 in the fireplace because of credit-card balances you accumulated years ago.

You'd probably say you have a spending problem. Washington calls it a budget.

JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

Roughly speaking, out of every $100 the federal government spent in 2025, about $23 went to Social Security, approximately $26 went toward major health programs, around $13 went toward national defense, and about $14 serviced the interest on our debt. The remaining dollars funded everything from veterans' benefits and income-security programs to transportation, education, federal agencies and thousands of other government programs.

You can argue all day about which of those programs are worthwhile. But here's the part Washington doesn't put on your receipt.

BILLIONAIRE BEZOS SUGGESTS NO TAXES FOR HALF THE NATION. IS THAT CRAZY OR OVERDUE?

Federal revenues were only about $5.2 trillion while spending approached $7 trillion. The result was another roughly $1.8 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025. In other words, for every $100 Washington spent, it collected only about $74 and borrowed roughly $26 to make up the difference.

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., addresses the House chamber of the U.S. Capitol after winning the speakership on Wednesday, Oct. 25, 2023. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Try that financial plan at your house. Earn $74. Spend $100. Put the other $26 on the credit card. Then do it again next year. And the year after that.

SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’

Eventually, your banker is going to have a conversation with you that nobody in Congress seems interested in having.

This isn't a Republican problem or a Democratic problem. It's an American math problem.

WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

Politicians love telling you about the benefits they're going to protect, the programs they're going to create and the taxes somebody else is supposedly going to pay. Nobody likes telling you the truth.

We have promised ourselves a government we aren't currently willing to pay for. And taxpayers should demand something that every restaurant, grocery store and hardware store already gives us.

Think about your own household budget. Imagine earning $100 and immediately throwing $14 in the fireplace because of credit-card balances you accumulated years ago. You'd probably say you have a spending problem. Washington calls it a budget.

Every year, Americans should be able to see exactly how Washington spent every $100 it collected and how much additional money it borrowed in our name.

Because here's the number that scares me most.

The Congressional Budget Office says net interest costs are projected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026 and could reach about $2.1 trillion annually by 2036 under current law.

That's money future taxpayers will send to Washington before Congress buys them a single bridge, missile or Medicare benefit. Americans argue constantly about whether our taxes are too high or too low. Maybe we're asking the wrong question.

Before Washington asks Americans for another dollar, taxpayers should be asking: What did you do with the last $100?

Ted Jenkin is President of Exit Stage Left Advisors and Host of The Red, White & Green Show.

articles.title: New Hampshire voters head to polls in race crucial to Democrats’ Senate hopes
articles.excerpt:
Centrist Chris Pappas faces progressive primary challenger Karishma Manzur while Republicans eye chance to flip seat

New Hampshire voters head to the polls Tuesday for primaries that will set up a cl...
articles.body_text:
Centrist Chris Pappas faces progressive primary challenger Karishma Manzur while Republicans eye chance to flip seat

New Hampshire voters head to the polls Tuesday for primaries that will set up a closely watched Senate contest – a vulnerable open seat Democrats must defend if they are to have any shot at reclaiming the upper chamber.

The race opened when Jeanne Shaheen, 79, the state’s three‑term incumbent Democratic senator, announced her retirement. Congressman Chris Pappas, who represents New Hampshire’s first district, is seeking the nomination and enters the final stretch with a clear financial edge: more than $4m cash on hand, according to his latest filings. But his main challenger, Dr Karishma Manzur – a scientist and progressive activist with no experience holding public office – has gained ground.

If he wins the primary, Pappas, 46, is likely to face the Donald Trump-endorsed former senator John E Sununu, who is seeking a return to the seat he once held and is part of a political dynasty that includes his father and brother, both former governors.

“This is the kind of place where you can’t just run a bunch of TV ads and expect to win,” Pappas told the Guardian. “You’ve got to meet people where they are. We’re finding support in corners you might not expect – including from people who voted for Trump last time but are open to a conversation about moving the country forward.”

A popular centrist, Pappas has served in the House since 2019 and has crossed the aisle at various points. He calls himself “battle‑tested” and has consolidated establishment backing, earning endorsements from leading Democratic lawmakers and former vice‑president Kamala Harris. His family’s name also carries weight in New Hampshire: the Pappases own the Puritan Backroom, the century‑old Manchester restaurant famed for allegedly inventing the chicken tender and long embedded in the state’s retail‑politics circuit.

Sununu, 61, is the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary, though he faces Scott Brown – another former senator who represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term.

The president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of the president, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary.

On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power, and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. He told New Hampshire Public Radio it was “a tactical mistake” to go to war “without having a plan for protecting the strait of Hormuz”. That posture may matter in a state where Trump’s approval rating sits at 38%.

Sununu and Brown did not respond to the Guardian’s interview requests.

Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said that Sununu was a “strong candidate” who was “well positioned to beat out Pappas” in a general election. “While Democrats have been consumed by infighting, Republicans have been laser-focused on real issues like affordability and security,” she added in a statement.

Some Democrats worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, the now-governor, captured a seat. Pappas insists he’s not taking anything for granted, and is running like he’s “10 votes behind” at all times – especially in a midterm cycle where progressive challengers have scored surprise primary wins across the country. This, however, hasn’t fazed Pappas who says he is running as a “New Hampshire Democrat” who knows his state.

But Manzur, who supports Medicare for All and higher taxes on mega‑corporations and the ultra‑wealthy, has repeatedly highlighted the money Pappas has received from donors aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. She casts him as milquetoast and ineffective. “I was tired of choosing between the lesser of two evils and still seeing so much pain and suffering right here in my state,” she said, calling both Pappas and Sununu “corporate politicians”.

“One has a ‘D’ after their name. One has an ‘R’ after their name … neither of them have been able to address the real needs of the people,” Manzur added.

Pappas, for his part, has long backed US aid to Israel but told the Guardian that Benjamin Netanyahu was “not a trustworthy ally of the US” and said he hoped the Israeli prime minister is ousted in the country’s October election. Pappas noted he has rejected corporate Pac money in this race but did not directly address his support from pro‑Israel donors, instead pointing to a “broad‑based effort” of individual contributors that have supported his Senate bid.

Pappas says he would support the Democratic nominee if he loses. “We need a big tent and new voices in the party to win tough elections,” he said at last week’s Democratic debate.

Manzur declined to make the same commitment. “I’m focused on winning,” she told the Guardian. “I’m not going to get into these discussions – they’re intentionally distracting from the people’s movement.”

Further down the ballot, the Democratic primary for Pappas’s House seat has drawn eight candidates, with Stefany Shaheen – daughter of the outgoing senator – and Maura Sullivan, a former Obama administration official, leading the field. The district, long purple, has been reliably blue since 2017. Republicans now see it as flippable, and Trump has endorsed Anthony DiLorenzo, a businessman who owns several car dealerships, in the GOP race.

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: What’s in an economy?
articles.excerpt: Janelle King, co-chair of Let's Win for America Action, dissects a recent Fox News poll revealing widespread economic dissatisfaction among voters. King explains that while President Trump highlights ...
articles.body_text:
Janelle King, co-chair of Let's Win for America Action, dissects a recent Fox News poll revealing widespread economic dissatisfaction among voters. King explains that while President Trump highlights "Trump accounts" as long-term benefits, voters are feeling immediate financial heat. She also expresses concern over the surging far-left influence in key Midwest primaries, noting a shift towards emotional voting.

Eight weeks from today, millions of Americans will choose their next congressperson. Poll after poll tells us that the state of the economy will shape their choice: it’s the top issue for voters by a wide margin and most Americans are in a sour mood about it.

We’ve learned from previous elections that voters consider a wide range of issues when they vote. The "economy" has different meanings to voters. Optimism doesn’t win over voters on pocketbook issues. And this year, while voters aren’t happy with President Donald Trump’s economy, that hasn't yet made them enthusiastic about the Democratic alternative.

These are the four rules to think about as we inch closer to the midterms.

Meantime, Democrats inch closer to victory as the Power Rankings takes a fresh look at congressional races in Missouri and Ohio.

The importance of the economy to elections has been a golden rule since the early '90s, when Democratic strategist James Carville famously cited "the economy, stupid" as the most important focus for a campaign.

Did you know it was only one of three orders he gave to candidates that cycle?

The economy has been a top-three issue throughout the Trump era, including the last two midterm elections, where it was the most important issue for 47% of voters (2022) and 18% of voters (2018).

If that 2018 figure feels low, it’s because healthcare (26%) and immigration (23%) finished ahead. That year, Republicans lost 42 seats.

No wonder another of Carville’s three rules for candidates was "don’t forget health care." (The third was "change vs more of the same.")

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

Fox News Power Rankings on President Donald Trump's economy. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

The state of the economy bleeds into other major concerns, including healthcare. But even a strong economy wasn’t enough to get the GOP out of that election unscathed. And healthcare looms as another important issue this year: it’s ranked close behind the economy in most surveys this year.

When pollsters ask about voters’ views on the economy, they usually ask how important "the economy" or "the state of the economy" is, or whether they’re satisfied with Trump’s performance on that issue.

In some important ways, Trump has a strong economic record. Just last week, the U.S. added 162,000 jobs, about triple what economists had expected. The unemployment rate was steady at 4.1%. The stock market also continues to grow, even as Iran and tariffs drive volatility.

These have helped keep Trump’s overall economic approval rating in the low-to-mid 30s in multiple polls this summer.

When pollsters ask only about Americans’ personal economic situation, things look tougher.

TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO'

Fox News Power Rankings on President Donald Trump's handling of issues. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

In a Reuters/Ipsos poll released last week, 32% of voters said they approved of Trump on the economy. But only a quarter approved of his performance on cost of living and 24% approved of him on inflation and prices.

The costs of gas, food and other basic goods are the major factors driving this discrepancy. If Democrats deliver a strong result in November, it will come down to a presidential approval rating in the mid-20s on these issues.

In 2022, President Joe Biden faced similar headwinds: the economy was rebounding, especially if you looked at unemployment, but inflation hovered around the 8% mark all year. Gas prices came in around $3.75.

The Biden administration kept selling the positives. First, inflation was "transitory." Then the president argued that "zero percent inflation" from one month to another was a win, despite the high annualized rate. Senior officials took victory laps on the unemployment rate.

Fox News Power Rankings on the economy in 2022 under former President Joe Biden. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Voters rejected this messaging at the ballot box, delivering the House to the GOP after a net loss of nine Democratic seats and handing Biden a net approval rating of -23 points on the economy.

Today, headline inflation is less than half that at 3.4%, while gas prices are a little higher at $4.15. Trump’s net approval on the economy currently sits at -33 points.

The Trump administration is running a familiar playbook. Vice President JD Vance said last week that gas prices could be worse if not for the Trump administration. As Fox’s Gillian Turner noted on "Special Report," there are similarities between a comment like that and the statements Biden officials made four years earlier.

These optimistic visions are likely to remain a tough sell to voters.

It’s easy to look at all this and think the Democrats are in for a big night in November. That’s certainly a possibility.

But polls keep showing that voters are just as discouraged by the left’s economic messaging.

FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS

Fox News Power Rankings on which party voters trust more to handle the economy. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Right now, Democrats are offering voters competing economic visions. Some, like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, want a revolution that starts with "Medicare-for-all" and higher taxes on the wealthy. Others say they want to undo Trump’s agenda while keeping the core of America’s economic system in place.

It’s not yet clear whether these visions are unappealing to voters or whether the contrast between them is the problem.

Either way, in the Reuters/Ipsos survey, 36% of voters say Republicans are the better party to handle the economy, while 37% prefer the Democrats. The poll has a ±3.3pt margin of error.

If the Republicans hold relatively steady in November – also a possibility in this forecast – those results will explain why.

Fox News Power Rankings forecast on the House of Representatives. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Democrats are still the favorites to take the House this November, with 212 seats in their columns to the GOP’s 206. There are 17 seats that are so close they could go either way.

Fox News Power Rankings forecast on the House of Representatives. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Those seats tend to swing in one direction as votes get counted. On a good night for Democrats, that means 229 seats, while a good night for the GOP would still see them hold onto their current House majority.

(A "great" night for either party would mean winning some of the seats that lean toward the opponent in this forecast. The Power Rankings puts seats in the "lean" category when they’re highly competitive, but one party has an edge.)

The changes in this forecast, which see two seats fall out of the GOP’s columns, all come from Missouri and Ohio.

Republicans picked up redistricting wins across the southeast after the Supreme Court’s ruling narrowing the scope of the Voting Rights Act this year.

That includes Missouri, where Republican lawmakers redrew the Kansas City-based 5th District, currently held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver, who won re-election there by 24 points, to include more White, rural areas.

That put the district into the Solid R column in the initial Power Rankings this year.

Last Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously blocked the new districts from being used unless voters approve them in a referendum. The order restores the state’s existing map, flipping Cleaver’s district back to Solid D.

MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP

Fox News Power Rankings forecast on the House of Representatives. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

(It also makes Missouri’s 2nd District more competitive. The rankings already had that district at Likely R; we’re keeping it there for now.)

Missouri has appealed the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which could rule on the state ruling quickly. For now, Cleaver holds on to the 5th District.

Three races in Ohio are heading leftward.

First, Ohio’s 7th District, held by Republican Max Miller. The congressman’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused Miller of physically abusing both her and their young daughter. Miller denies the allegations and has suggested Moreno has mental health issues.

Moreno is the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, who Miller says is trying to take down his political career.

The 7th District was already close for the ‘likely’ column, and after these headlines and some prodding from Republicans to drop out, it’s become highly competitive. It moves from Likely R to Toss Up.

Fox News Power Rankings forecast on the House of Representatives. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Meanwhile, in the southwest of the state, watch the 10th and 15th Districts, held by Republicans Mike Turner and Mike Carey, respectively.

These shouldn’t be part of the Democratic playbook in a regular election year: they’re predominantly White and middle-class.

Turner’s 10th District contains Dayton and some suburban areas; Carey’s 15th includes some suburban and exurban parts around Columbus and stretches to the rural south.

Fox News Power Rankings forecast on the House of Representatives. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

As the Fox News Poll has shown twice now, Democrat Sherrod Brown is running a strong race for Senate; up eight points at 53% in May and August. That kind of performance could create a closer race than Republicans would like.

The "Mikes" have the clear advantage, but victory isn’t a sure thing. The 10th and 15th Districts move from Solid R to Likely R.

Rémy Numa is the lead political affairs specialist for Fox News Channel. You can follow him on Twitter: @remynuma.

articles.title: Sadiq Khan rounds on Westminster council for keeping ‘vertical drinking’ curbs on pubs
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: London mayor accuses council of ‘breathtaking arrogance’ in ‘ignoring’ responses to a consultation

Sadiq Khan has criticised the “breathtaking arrogance” of Westminster council, which has ...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: London mayor accuses council of ‘breathtaking arrogance’ in ‘ignoring’ responses to a consultation

Sadiq Khan has criticised the “breathtaking arrogance” of Westminster council, which has kept restrictions on vertical drinking in Soho and an effective ban on new bars and pubs in the area.

The mayor of London has accused the Conservative-led council of “ignoring” the responses to a consultation into its new licensing policy. The vast majority of respondents, 81%, disagreed with the council’s “cumulative impact zone” which decrees that applications for bars and pubs in the West End of London, one of Europe’s most famous nightlife districts, will be refused unless in exceptional circumstances. Eighty-four per cent said the licensing policy would be bad for business.

Respondents also criticised the council’s position on “vertical drinking”, which is standing up to have a beverage, a common practice in British pubs. The council proposed, to widespread outcry, that new licences for pubs and bars should be granted to those venues which have table service instead of ordering at the bar, and those in which people are seated rather than standing.

The mayor had responded to a consultation held this summer by the council and ordered them to scrap the cumulative impact zone and allow pubs and bars to have space for vertical drinking. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, also waded into the row, saying vertical drinking is “British life”.

Despite this, the council is continuing with both the vertical drinking policy and the cumulative impact zone, and said that those who wrote to complain did so because they did not understand the terminology in its licensing document.

Khan told the Guardian: “The arrogance of Westminster council is breathtaking. By ignoring all those who oppose their plans and viewing hospitality in the heart of our capital city as a problem, they are letting down businesses, residents and our economy. They would rather see nightlife die than thrive.”

Tim Barnes, Westminster city council’s deputy leader, said the issue was a policing one and called for more resources for the area. He added: “Beyond disagreements over policy jargon there are serious issues acting as a drag on our hospitality industry.

“A lack of investment in policing has left the Met objecting to many licensing applications over public safety concerns.”

But the final licensing policy keeps restrictions on vertical drinking. It reads: “When considering new licence applications, discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking.”

In the revised policy, the council says it did approve a new pub in the cumulative impact zone recently – The Lady in Covent Garden. However, most of the space in this pub is for a sit-down restaurant. The document states that the bar on the bottom floor of the pub would not usually be allowed, but in this case it is because it will “only operate in association with the restaurant use”.

The government is due to grant new powers to the Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes.

He said: “London’s famous hospitality and nightlife sectors are vital for our economy, and one of the reasons our capital is so special.

“Running our world-famous nightlife district with a nimby village-hall mindset is simply not sustainable. This is why the government was right to give me new powers to help ensure our fantastic hospitality and nightlife can flourish, helping create more jobs and ensure we stay a vibrant global city.”

Data shows that only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026. Pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24.

The Soho Society, a group established in 1972 aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”, voted in its AGM earlier this summer for a new licensing mandate, meaning it will challenge all new applications for bars and restaurants in the area, including reviews of existing licences. It will also object to any venue that wishes to open beyond “core hours”, which Westminster council decrees end between 10.30pm and midnight, depending on the business and day of the week.

articles.title: Trey McKinney says Bassmaster veterans made him earn their respect before historic AOY season
articles.excerpt: 2026 Bassmaster Angler of the Year Trey McKinney tells OutKick OutDoors what it was like entering the Bassmaster Elite Series as a young rookie, earning respect from veteran anglers and finally feelin...
articles.body_text:
2026 Bassmaster Angler of the Year Trey McKinney tells OutKick OutDoors what it was like entering the Bassmaster Elite Series as a young rookie, earning respect from veteran anglers and finally feeling like he belongs among the sport’s best.

Trey McKinney has spent most of his professional fishing career being the youngest guy in the room.

And apparently, the Bassmaster Elite Series veterans weren't exactly waiting at the dock with open arms.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

McKinney arrived on the Elite Series as a teenager and immediately started making noise. Now, at just 21 years old, he's already a former Rookie of the Year, the youngest Elite Series winner in history and, as of last weekend, the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year ever.

Trey McKinney celebrates his Bassmaster Angler of the Year win with friends and family. (Amber Harding Snyder)

But according to McKinney, earning all those accolades was one thing. Earning the respect of the other Elites took a little longer.

"They're not a very welcoming crew to begin with," McKinney told OutKick OutDoors. "If you're somebody that's coming on the Elite Series, don't expect a warm hand of, 'Come on, buddy. The water's warm. Come on in. It's a great time.'"

McKinney isn't complaining about it. In fact, he thinks that's probably how it should be.

"Rookies coming in, you get a hard time. You've got to learn how to prove yourself," he said. "And once you do that, it honestly makes it that much sweeter."

Watch Trey McKinney's full interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

For McKinney, proving himself happened quickly on paper. He finished second in the Angler of the Year standings in each of his first two Elite seasons, both times behind Chris Johnston.

But he said the first couple of years were still a "hard road" when it came to being accepted by the veterans around him.

"This year, it's kind of watching things turn around a little bit, gaining respect from certain people that I would never see it from," McKinney said. "Now that I see that they respect me, I respect them just as much. So it's very mutual."

He laughed while describing just how different those interactions are now.

"Now I can go out and have a normal conversation with somebody, and they don't just — I'm like, 'Hey,' and they just turn around and walk off," he said. "Now we can have a conversation like man to man, and it's pretty special to see where it was to where it is now."

In other words, he's not just the kid anymore.

"Exactly," McKinney said. "I feel more welcome. I feel like I'm out there having fun. We're doing our job. We're competing. We're competitors, and we realize that. But at the same time, we have the same respect as we do for everybody."

If there were any doubts left about whether McKinney belonged among the sport's best, he pretty well erased them on the St. Lawrence River.

RICKEY JACKSON WINS FIRST BASSMASTER RANDY MOSS PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME PRO-AM ON ST. LAWRENCE RIVER

McKinney entered the final Elite Series event of the season with the Angler of the Year title within reach. He then caught a 30-pound, 11-ounce five-fish smallmouth limit on Day 2 — the heaviest in Bassmaster history — and put himself in position not only to win AOY but also to win the tournament.

By Sunday morning, however, the normally cool 21-year-old was feeling every ounce of what was at stake.

"I'd never been so nervous that it affected my fishing, really," McKinney said. "But no, it really did that last day."

There was a tournament win, $200,000 and the title he'd spent three years chasing all hanging on one final eight-hour day.

Trey McKinney chats on stage while holding his 2026 Angler of the Year trophy. (Amber Harding Snyder)

"I'd be lying if I said it didn't affect me because it did," he said. "I just didn't fish very good. I got nervous. I got impatient. I wanted it to be over quickly, and it just wasn't."

The fish weren't cooperating early, either.

McKinney hit his first few spots and came away with little to show for it. That's when the thoughts started creeping in.

"There's no way I've got all the way here. I've got a good pound cushion. I'm leading the tournament. There's no way I'm letting it slip through my hands. Not this time," he recalled thinking. "I added a lot of pressure to myself, I feel like, more than I should have."

That pressure was especially understandable considering how close he'd already come twice.

Strangely enough, those two previous runner-up finishes had actually helped him stay loose for most of the week.

"I was like, 'You know what? It is what it is. We've been here twice. What's going to happen? Get second again?'" McKinney said. "It kind of took the pressure off of us."

"All the work we have done literally has come down to this last eight hours, and that's where it all hit me," he said.

Eventually, McKinney landed a 6-pounder, and everything changed.

"Everything was good. Everything was all right, and we fished like normal Trey," he said.

McKinney ultimately finished second in the tournament, but it was more than enough to secure the Angler of the Year title.

And there was some poetic justice in who handed him the trophy.

Johnston, the man who had finished ahead of McKinney in the AOY race in each of the previous two seasons, was there to present it.

McKinney has plenty of respect for Johnston, whom he called an "unbelievable angler." He also admitted he enjoyed finally getting the better of him.

"He beat me fair and square. It is what it was," McKinney said. "But it did feel good to finally get one on him. Like, 'Hey, yeah, you've had the last two years. This one's mine.'"

Trey McKinney holds up his "Century Club" belt after bagging more than 100 pounds of bass during the four-day tournament. (Amber Harding Snyder)

With the win, McKinney broke a record that had stood since 1992, when Kevin VanDam became Bassmaster Angler of the Year at 24 years old.

McKinney said he didn't even realize until recently that he was still young enough to take that record from the man he called "pretty much the greatest of all time."

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Safe to say, McKinney has earned his place.

At this point, nobody on the Elite Series should need much more convincing.

Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more states
articles.excerpt:
Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory

‘It breaks my heart’: victory sparks dismay

Thousands of Germans have staged protests a...
articles.body_text:
Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory

‘It breaks my heart’: victory sparks dismay

Thousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month.

Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting.

The party captured its best-ever state result in the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September.

Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”.

With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result.

The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the best for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage.

Wagner sounded the alarm that the AfD, although it fell just short of an absolute majority, was on the brink of taking power in Saxony-Anhalt, a first for the far right since the second world war. That “should not be accepted in silence”, he said.

Max Schneller, 17, a member of the far-left Linke, from Saxony-Anhalt, said activists in the state would fight any attempts by an AfD government to target minorities. “We will not start categorising our neighbours according to their origin, religion or skin colour – we are too humane to hate,” he said to loud applause.

The AfD is three votes short of the support necessary to form a government under its candidate, the media-savvy firebrand Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to peel off dissenters from the remaining parties willing to play kingmaker.

Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has since 2023 listed the state chapter of the party as right-wing extremist, saying it poses a threat to democratic norms.

Hundreds of anti-AfD protesters also gathered in Potsdam, near Berlin, with rallies also organised in Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt, and Halberstadt, in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD captured nearly half the votes, local media reported.

In Halle, the region’s second largest city, leftist groups and civil society organisations have been staging a protest camp since election day.

The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%. However, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) of the state premier, Manuela Schwesig, mounted a remarkable comeback over the summer and is now scoring above 30%.

In Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the picture is more mixed, with several parties jockeying for first place. It is governed by a coalition of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the SPD.

The CDU, the party of chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose record unpopularity is reported to have weighed heavily with voters in Saxony-Anhalt, holds a wafer-thin lead in the capital, with about 20%.

Hot on its heels is the Linke, which has focused on soaring housing costs in its campaign, and the AfD, followed by the SPD and the ecologist Greens, both polling in the mid-teens.

Merz has vowed to stay in office and fight for a signature package of painful reforms, arguing the only way to defeat the AfD is to get Europe’s top economy moving again and repair its creaking social welfare system.

However the SPD, his junior coalition partner, has indicated its willingness to backtrack on some of the most unpopular measures to shore up support for the embattled government.

Analysts say the dispute could further destabilise the shaky coalition.

articles.title: Liverpool announce five-year shirt sponsorship deal with Turkish Airlines
articles.excerpt: Liverpool have ‌agreed a five-year deal for Turkish Airlines to ⁠become their ⁠main club partner from June 1, 2027, which means the first change in the Anfield side’s ⁠leading shirt sponsor since 2010...
articles.body_text:
Liverpool have ‌agreed a five-year deal for Turkish Airlines to ⁠become their ⁠main club partner from June 1, 2027, which means the first change in the Anfield side’s ⁠leading shirt sponsor since 2010, ending a 17-year run for Standard Chartered.

The deal announced on Tuesday will ⁠be worth in excess of 300 million pounds ($405.78m) according to media reports, which would place it among the most lucrative in the Premier League.

While the precise figures have not been ‌confirmed, it is likely to match the income from Manchester United’s shirt sponsorship deal with Qualcomm, which was signed in August 2024.

Standard Chartered will remain affiliated with Liverpool as a Global Partner, said a club statement, but Turkish Airlines will take the primary position ⁠in Liverpool’s branding.

“The front of the ⁠Liverpool shirt holds a special place in the history of our club,” said Liverpool’s chief commercial officer Ben Latty.

“Turkish Airlines is a globally ⁠recognised organisation with an extensive international network and we look forward to beginning ⁠our partnership and building a strong ⁠relationship together, with already strong foundations built from those special memories back in 2005,” he added, referring to Liverpool’s Champions League final comeback ‌win in Istanbul.

The deal adds to a growing sponsorship portfolio within football for Turkish Airlines, who are an ‌official ‌partner of the Champions League and main sponsor of Turkiye’s national team.

In February, Liverpool announced record revenues of more than 700 million pounds ($950m) for the most recent financial year, and were the highest-placed Premier League club in the Deloitte Football Money League.

Liverpool were the first major English professional football club to have a shirt sponsor, when Japanese electronics company Hitachi had its name displayed across the club’s strip back in 1979.

articles.title: Qatar says reopening Strait of Hormuz ‘unconditionally’ is a priority
articles.excerpt:
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson says “new ideas are being discussed” between Qatar and other mediators for ways to resolve the more than six-month US-Iran war.

“It’s not acceptable a...
articles.body_text:
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson says “new ideas are being discussed” between Qatar and other mediators for ways to resolve the more than six-month US-Iran war.

“It’s not acceptable at all to have this state of no war and no peace. This is not beneficial to the region, the countries of the region, and the people,” Ibrahim Al Hashmi, director of the media department at Qatar’s Foreign Ministry, said on Tuesday.

“Qatar is working hard with its partners, including China. Diplomatic efforts are being exerted and new ideas are being discussed,” he said.

Qatar’s Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani met Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing on Tuesday, where they discussed enhancing security and stability in the region and solutions for the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

“I had a fruitful meeting with my friend, HE Wang Yi, Foreign Minister of China. We discussed strengthening bilateral relations to serve our mutual interests, reviewed regional and international developments, and looked forward to working together for international peace and security,” Qatar’s prime minister said on X.

Al Hashmi said “the most important thing is to have political will with both parties to resolve the problem,” referring to Iran and the US.

He added that “Qatar and the countries of the region are quite keen for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz unconditionally because this is a top priority.”

The Foreign Ministry spokesperson also discussed the war in Yemen, where fighting between forces loyal to the Saudi Arabia-backed internationally recognised government and Houthi rebels escalated last week, with the Houthis also launching attacks on Saudi territory.

Al Hashmi said Qatar condemned “the attack of Houthis on civilian institutions in Abha, Jizan, and Najran, and Khamis Mushait”.

The Houthi attacks have “led to the injury of so many civilians and this has led to problems with shipments in the Red Sea and is a threat to international navigation”, the spokesman added.

articles.title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
articles.excerpt:
In strongest condemnation ever by UK government, Ed Miliband announces sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements

Israeli “terrorists” are conducting ethnic cleansing in the West Bank with ...
articles.body_text:
In strongest condemnation ever by UK government, Ed Miliband announces sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements

Israeli “terrorists” are conducting ethnic cleansing in the West Bank with the tacit backing of the government, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has said as he announced sweeping sanctions, alongside France and Canada, on trade with Israeli settlements.

In the strongest condemnation ever issued by the UK government, Miliband said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, saying such acknowledgment was “the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”

Miliband said that the government would now enact:

An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.

A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements.

A ban on the advertising in the UK of illegal settlement properties.

Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.

A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

Miliband said the action would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.

The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

Miliband said those who financed or facilitated illegal settlements would “face the full force of UK sanctions” and that he expected the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months.

He stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians. I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”

He said the British government had previously described settlements as illegal but had not described the occupation itself as unlawful, and that would now change.

France and Canada were also announcing bans on settlement goods on Tuesday, joining the Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway, which have either banned goods or were in the process of doing so.

Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust.

“I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.

“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”

He said to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

Miliband said he felt a “deep sense of shame about what has unfolded in Palestine under the eyes of the international community” and said there had been “the most unimaginable trauma and suffering in the last three years – death, destruction and dehumanisation on an appalling scale”.

The foreign secretary said the action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine; one that not only condemned but took action.

“Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”

Miliband said the actions of the Israeli government in the West Bank meant more settlements had been approved in the last four years than in the last 20 years combined.

He said he believed the majority of the British people would support the ban on trade with illegal settlements. “Settlements are illegal. They should not be promoted in our country,” he said.

The UK government knew there were also concerns about arm sales to Israel, he said. The UK had already suspended more than 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza, but would now go further.

“We will now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation, in effect a double lock against arms sales. This means the ban on such exports will now remain as long as the occupation persists.”

He said the UK would support “full, robust and fair judicial processes” to determine if Israel had committed genocide and said the government would not pre-judge that process.

“This has been the case for all of the genocides since the 1948 genocide convention: Rwanda, Srebrenica, Cambodia, and acts against the Yazidi people. This will remain our policy. It is right that this issue has been brought before the ICJ [international court of justice] and I want to make it clear that we support the court in coming to its determination.”

However, he said that the most recent reports by international bodies found there was “increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed and we support legal processes to determine this”.

The UK would use the UN general assembly next week to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change”.

The steps set out by Miliband fall short of the full demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but are a sign the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies, such as Qatar, on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.

Both the US and Israel have threatened retaliation against Britain for the sanctions. The US ambassador to Israel, Mick Huckabee, said the US was considering what action to take, warning it may prohibit the UK from trade with several US states that have anti-BDS (boycott, divestment, sanctions) laws.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was “a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation” before the country’s elections in October.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, said: “If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain,” and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, called for the expulsion of the British ambassador.

articles.title: Lane Kiffin goes full villain mode during alleged halftime speech from LSU's blowout win over Clemson
articles.excerpt: "This is what you wanted. And now you're mad at no rules? You're full of *hit. No, you are everybody. Not everybody. But I've heard 3 or 4 coaches use the word 'embarrassing.’ I'm looking at my phone....
articles.body_text:
"This is what you wanted. And now you're mad at no rules? You're full of *hit. No, you are everybody. Not everybody. But I've heard 3 or 4 coaches use the word 'embarrassing.’ I'm looking at my phone. Embarrassing them. Embarrassing? What the hell is so embarrassing about it? What, you're going to run out there? There's going to be, however many people in your little hellhole of a college you're going to collect, I don't think you're embarrassed to take that check. Are you, big boy? I think that checks going direct deposit.

LSU sent a clear message, not only to Clemson, but to the entire country with its dominant first-half performance against the visiting Tigers in Week 1 by taking a 31-3 lead into the break. Thirty minutes of complete control was not enough for LSU head coach Lane Kiffin, however, not nearly enough, in fact.

With Kiffin's offseason bookended by a nasty exit from Ole Miss and court cases involving former NFL players potentially returning to college and suiting up for the Bayou Bengals, LSU and its newest head coach didn't exactly enter the season as 'America's Team.'

Someone has to claim the role of college football's biggest villain, and the most polarizing coach in the sport, leading a team that reportedly costs north of $40 million in NIL money and partnering with unsavory storylines galore.

Lane Kiffin, head coach of the LSU Tigers on the field before a game against the Clemson Tigers at Tiger Stadium on September 5, 2026 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

TIME IS NOW, CLEMSON TIGERS AND DABO SWINNEY NEED TO CALL IT QUITS AFTER HISTORIC RUN

Through one game of the season, Kiffin and LSU aren't only thriving while playing the big bad villain, but fully embracing it.

Kiffin's alleged halftime speech from LSU's win over Clemson has leaked, and the message revealed a coach and a program fully leaning into the narrative that they're the most-hated in the sport.

LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin on the sideline during the third quarter of a game against the Clemson Tigers on September 5, 2026, at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

LSU FANS BOO JAYDEN DANIELS DURING JUMBOTRON TRIBUTE AFTER NIL CEASE-AND-DESIST DISPUTE

"Alright, guys, we started here like seven, eight months ago, whatever it was," Kiffin said in the video. "We asked you to work really hard. We asked you to come back to work again and again and again. Do you feel good about what happened? Who gives a f— what happened? That’s what’s supposed to happen. There’s no f—ing celebrations for that. They’re f—ing soft.

"So you’ve got to show them again. They’re going to come out. It doesn’t matter what plays they run. It doesn’t matter what they do on offense, defense. Put the next motherf—ing quarterback in. I don’t give a f—. You send them a f–ing message who the f— is on their schedule. They have to play you.

"And don’t think we’re letting up late. No matter if you’re in the game for one more snap or 50 more snaps, you f—ing take it out on them. The whole f—ing world hates you. So you get a chance to show the whole world, ‘Go f— yourself.’ Clemson just had to see it right now."

LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffen walks the sideline during a game between the LSU Tigers and the Clemson Tigers on September 5, 2026, at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by John Korduner/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (John Korduner/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Not only was LSU up 31-3 when Kiffin delivered the alleged speech, but the Tigers had held Clemson to just 54 total yards of offense on 25 plays and negative four yards on the ground.

Kiffin's message was delivered loud and clear, as LSU went on to outscore Clemson 20-7 in the second half to earn a 51-10 victory. LSU outgained Clemson by a stunning 499 yards on offense when it was all said and done.

articles.title: UK announces sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
articles.excerpt:
United Kingdom Foreign Minister Ed Miliband has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Britain will ⁠introduce an import ban on goods ⁠from Israeli settlements,...
articles.body_text:
United Kingdom Foreign Minister Ed Miliband has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Britain will ⁠introduce an import ban on goods ⁠from Israeli settlements, Miliband told parliament on Tuesday.

He said that there will also be a comprehensive sanctions regime put in place, adding that Britain could no longer simply “call out” injustice and suffering, but told the House of Commons that the country now had to “act” to oppose the expansion of settlements.

“Today we refuse to be bystanders to further suffering and to the destruction of the two-state solution,” Miliband said, referring to Britain’s long-held support for the two-state idea, which Israel opposes.

The United States, through its ambassador to Israel, has already criticised Britain’s plan to impose sanctions, while two Israeli ministers called for measures to be taken against Britain.

Miliband, who became Britain’s foreign minister in July, also said Britain’s position is that the occupation in the West Bank is unlawful, and that London believes that there is “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank.

The impact on the £6 billion ($8.12bn) of annual bilateral trade between the UK and Israel is likely to be minimal, with details unclear of how the UK will differentiate between goods originating in West Bank settlements and products made in Israel.

articles.title: Sudan’s healthcare system on brink of collapse, MSF warns
articles.excerpt: War-torn Sudan’s healthcare system is facing a deep crisis as international aid funding has dwindled, cutting millions off from essential services, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initial...
articles.body_text:
War-torn Sudan’s healthcare system is facing a deep crisis as international aid funding has dwindled, cutting millions off from essential services, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, has warned.

The medical charity said on Tuesday that a greater number of patients are being pushed towards a shrinking number of facilities, even as certain regions have seen intensifying violence and displacement with the country’s war escalating.

It urged governments at the United Nations General Assembly, which is currently convening, to protect health funding and provide stopgap financing for facilities at risk of closing.

About 37 percent of Sudan’s health facilities are out of service and the UN’s response plan for the country is only 41 percent funded, MSF said, with some 19.5 million people facing crisis levels of hunger earlier this year.

Mohammad Ibrahim, head of MSF in Sudan, says the organisation has been overwhelmed as funding for other aid efforts disappears.

“Donors must protect essential health services and provide sustained, flexible funding to organisations that depend on it,” he says in the report.

Fabrizio Locuratolo, humanitarian affairs manager at an MSF hospital in Um Rakuba, says the cuts extend beyond healthcare.

“Food rations are shrinking and protection programmes are being dismantled, pulling away the last safety nets and leaving refugees completely exposed,” he said.

MSF linked the closures to the shutdown of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), whose Sudan grants ended in June, and a significant reduction of aid from European institutions year-over-year.

The report notes that the world is witnessing “historic international aid funding cuts by governments”, with global humanitarian aid reduced by 35.8 percent since last year.

The war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed at least 59,000 people and displaced about 14 million since it erupted in April 2023.

articles.title: 4 family members flying from Bahamas to Florida in small plane go missing, with Coast Guard joining search
articles.excerpt: The 'Fox & Friends' hosts review dramatic footage of 23-year-old pilot Faith Tenkley surviving an emergency water landing off the coast of Boca Raton, Florida, on August 22. Tenkley successfully guide...
articles.body_text:
The 'Fox & Friends' hosts review dramatic footage of 23-year-old pilot Faith Tenkley surviving an emergency water landing off the coast of Boca Raton, Florida, on August 22. Tenkley successfully guides her single-engine aircraft away from beachgoers and paddleboarders before swimming safely to shore, earning praise from local authorities for her quick and professional decision-making.

The U.S. Coast Guard has joined the search for a plane carrying four Florida family members that authorities in the Bahamas believe "crash-landed" in the ocean after departing from Great Harbour Cay.

Pilot Mario Lamar, 80, his wife Lili, 79, and two of their grandchildren, Sofia Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22, were identified by family as those on board the PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft that was heading to Opa-locka, Florida, according to the Miami Herald.

"Please help," Silvia Larrieu, the niece of the couple, told the newspaper. "I ask anybody out there, if you can help with search and rescue efforts, we would greatly appreciate it. We need to bring them home."

Larrieu said the four were coming home to Florida after visiting a vacation property in Great Harbour Cay over Labor Day weekend and that "they’ve spent their whole life going there." Data from the website FlightAware showed the plane descended from 10,000 feet to 3,700 feet in about three minutes before vanishing from radar.

AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY

Great Harbour Cay in the Bahamas is seen from an airplane during a flight from Spain to the Caribbean. (NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Larrieu told the Miami Herald that Mario Lamar had years of experience as a pilot and always kept the aircraft in "pristine" shape.

U.S. Coast Guard Southeast said Monday it was assisting authorities in the Bahamas "following a report of a downed aircraft with four souls on board approx 15 mi off Andros Island," with a Coast Guard HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane joining the search.

The Royal Bahamas Police Force said it received a report around 2:20 p.m. on Monday "that an aircraft may have gone down in the waters off Red Bays."

COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY ONBOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE

A U.S. Coast Guard HC-144 Ocean Sentry medium-range surveillance plane from Air Station Cape Cod flies over the Atlantic Ocean in Newport, R.I., on April 4, 2026. One of these planes has joined the search for the missing aircraft off the coast of the Bahamas. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
